title: Kanya puja: girls as the Goddess
hook: a pot of earth with seeds, a fast, and on the eighth day small girls seated and fed as the Goddess
carry: kanya puja: every girl honored as the goddess
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the universe in a baby's mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri's book: the gods' hymn to the Goddess in all beings. Your line: shakti. The Goddess lives in all beings as power.

It's the first morning of Navaratri in an apartment in Delhi. Before breakfast, someone spreads a layer of soil in a shallow tray and scatters barley over it. In the middle goes a clay pot of water, mango leaves tucked around its neck, a coconut on top. A lamp is lit beside it. Then everyone leaves for work and school. There's nothing to see yet, just a pot and some dirt. But by the ninth day, that tray will be a small field of green.
screen: `FIRST MORNING: SOIL AND SEEDS.` → `A POT, MANGO LEAVES, A COCONUT.` → `BY THE NINTH DAY: GREEN.`

segments.voice: Start at the end of the Goddess's book. The last demon king has fallen, and the gods, saved, sing her one more hymn of thanks. In it they say something families still act out: every kind of knowledge is a form of you, Goddess, and so is every woman in the world. And she answers with a promise: whenever trouble rises, call me, and I'll come again. Navaratri is that calling. It opens with ghatasthapana. Ghata, the pot. Sthapana, setting it up. Many families invite the Goddess to be present in that pot for the nine days, and sow barley beside it, jau in Hindi. Many fast, some until evening, many by setting grain aside for buckwheat, fruit and milk. Then, on the eighth or ninth day, comes the custom that surprises people most. Families invite young girls from the neighborhood into the house. They wash the girls' feet, mark their foreheads, seat them like honored guests and feed them, often puri, chickpeas and a sweet halwa, with a small gift at the end. It's called kanya puja, and the girls are honored as forms of the Goddess herself. That's the teaching, said plainly. The Goddess isn't only in the pot or on the shrine. Her power is honored in living girls and women, the ones at your own table. Many teachers draw the harder lesson too: a girl worshiped on the eighth night can't be treated as less on any other day. On the tenth day comes Vijayadashami, the victory, and in some homes the green shoots are handed out as a blessing.
screen: `THE GODS' LAST HYMN.` · `EVERY WOMAN IS A FORM OF YOU.` · `GHATASTHAPANA: THE POT, THE SEEDS.` · `KANYA PUJA: GIRLS AS THE GODDESS.` · then, large: `HONORED AT YOUR OWN TABLE.`

segments.voice: Picture the eighth morning: small girls in bright clothes on a mat, a brass plate, a pitcher of warm water. If you pray, pour the water over a small pair of feet in your mind, and say Jai Mata Di. If you don't, think of one girl or woman whose strength goes unthanked, a sister, a teacher, a grandmother, and choose one real way to honor her this week.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with a pot and seeds, a fast, girls honored as her forms, and the tenth day's victory.
Your line: kanya puja. Every girl honored as the Goddess. Day one hundred forty-four, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus open Navaratri by setting up a pot as the Goddess's seat and sowing barley beside it, fast on some or all of the nine days, honor young girls as the Goddess in kanya puja on the eighth or ninth day, and keep the nights with garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal and golu dolls in the South, ending on Vijayadashami.

original.note: Sanskrit: nava, nine, and ratri, night. many say navratri in Hindi and Gujarati.

what it means: nine nights of calling the Goddess: a pot and sprouting seeds at home, a fast, and young girls honored as her forms, because her power lives in girls and women.

what a scholar hears: in the Devi Mahatmya's eleventh chapter the gods sing that all knowledge and all women are forms of the Devi, and she promises to return when called; kanya puja on ashtami or navami honors young girls as Devi, and ghatasthapana makes the pot her seat.

ghatasthapana.meaning: setting up the sacred pot on Navaratri's first morning

jau.meaning: barley, sown beside the pot and watched as it sprouts

kanya puja.meaning: honoring young girls as forms of the Goddess

garba.meaning: Gujarat's circle dance around a lamp

golu.meaning: dolls set out on steps in the South

notes: Ghatasthapana details (clay pot, coconut, mango leaves, barley/jau sown in soil) vary by family and region. Confirm.
Fasting 'without grain' during Navaratri is common in North India; practice varies. Confirm.
Durga Puja: the image as a daughter (Uma) visiting her parents' home; immersion (bisarjan) on Dashami. Confirm.
Golu (Tamil Nadu), Bombe Habba (Karnataka), Bommala Koluvu (Andhra): 'Tamil Nadu and Karnataka' named. Confirm, and whether to name the local names.
Kanya puja on Ashtami or Navami. Confirm.
Dussehra effigy burning connects to Rama's victory over Ravana, a different story from Durga's; mentioned without explaining. A Keeper may want a sentence making that clear.
